The oracle arm runs\n# the script from /solution while the dataset is mounted read-only at /app/data, so\n# solve.sh overrides this with --datadir.\nDATA_DIR = os.path.join(HERE, 'data')\n\n# trial window relative to the go cue, and bin width, in seconds\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 1.5\nBIN = 0.05\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             # 80\n\nREL_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)         # 81 edges, re go cue\nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        # 80 bin centres\n\nOUTCOME_CODE = {'ignore': 0, 'miss': 1, 'hit': 2}\nEARLY_CODE = {'no early': 0, 'early': 1}\nSIDE_CODE = {'left': 0, 'right': 1}\nCHOICE_NO_LICK = 2               # no lick in the response window\nTONGUE_HIDDEN = 3                # no visible tongue frame in the bin\n\nTONGUE_CONF = 0.5                # tracking likelihood for the tongue to count as visible\nTONGUE_PCT = (40, 60)            # per-session percentiles -> 3 visible classes\n\nINPUT_NAMES = ['time_from_tone_onset', 'photostim']\nOUTPUT_NAMES = ['choice', 'outcome', 'early_lick', 'tongue_y_position']\n\n# output_values[i][code] names each value of output i\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ['left', 'right', 'no lick'],\n    ['ignore', 'miss', 'hit'],\n    ['no', 'yes'],\n    ['below 40th pct', '40th to 60th pct', 'above 60th pct', 'not visible'],\n]\n\n\ndef region_label(anno):\n    \"\"\"'Orbital area, lateral part, layer 5' -> 'orbital area'.\"\"\"\n    return re.split(r'[,./]', anno)[0].strip().lower()\n\n\ndef _text(col):\n    \"\"\"Read a text column; non-str entries (unlabelled sessions) become ''.\"\"\"\n    return np.array([x if isinstance(x, str) else '' for x in col[:]])\n\n\ndef _bin_mean(idx, y, n):\n    \"\"\"Mean of y per bin given a per-sample bin index. NaN where a bin is empty.\"\"\"\n    ok = ~np.isnan(y)\n    tot = np.bincount(idx[ok], weights=y[ok], minlength=n)\n    cnt = np.bincount(idx[ok], minlength=n)\n    with np.errstate(invalid='ignore'):\n        return np.where(cnt > 0, tot / np.maximum(cnt, 1), np.nan)\n\n\ndef tongue_output(nwb, go):\n    \"\"\"Discretise tongue y into (n_trials, N_BINS) classes.\"\"\"\n    ts = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series['Camera0_side_TongueTracking']\n    t_cam = np.asarray(ts.timestamps)\n    data = ts.data[:]                        # (n_frames, 3) = x, y, likelihood\n    y = data[:, 1].copy()\n    y[data[:, 2] < TONGUE_CONF] = np.nan     # keep only visible frames\n\n    # bin the whole session on one grid, then take percentiles of the bin means\n    gidx = np.floor((t_cam - t_cam[0]) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n    edges = np.nanpercentile(_bin_mean(gidx, y, int(gidx[-1]) + 1), TONGUE_PCT)\n\n    # per trial, bin the same way and digitise against those edges\n    cls = np.full((len(go), N_BINS), TONGUE_HIDDEN, np.int8)\n    lo = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_START, 'left')\n    hi = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_STOP, 'left')\n    for i in range(len(go)):\n        b = np.floor((t_cam[lo[i]:hi[i]] - (go[i] + T_START)) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n        np.clip(b, 0, N_BINS - 1, out=b)\n        m = _bin_mean(b, y[lo[i]:hi[i]], N_BINS)\n        ok = ~np.isnan(m)\n        cls[i, ok] = np.digitize(m[ok], edges)\n    return cls\n\n\ndef process_session(path):\n    \"\"\"Convert one NWB file. an early lick replays the sample epoch\n        sample = np.asarray(bev['sample_start_times'].timestamps)\n        tone = sample[np.searchsorted(sample, go, side='left') - 1]\n\n        # ---- inputs --------------------------------------------------------\n        # bins sit around the go cue, values are seconds since the tone\n        time_from_tone = CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone)[:, None]\n\n        # photostim onsets are stored as strings relative to trial start\n        on_s = trials['photostim_onset'].values\n        has = on_s != 'N/A'\n        stim_on = np.full(n_trials, np.nan)\n        stim_on[has] = trials['start_time'].values[has] + on_s[has].astype(float) - go[has]\n        stim_off = np.full(n_trials, np.nan)\n        stim_off[has] = stim_on[has] + trials['photostim_duration'].values[has].astype(float)\n        # NaN compares False, so non-stim trials stay 0\n        photostim = ((CENTERS[None, :] >= stim_on[:, None])\n                     & (CENTERS[None, :] < stim_off[:, None]))\n\n        inp = np.stack([time_from_tone, photostim], axis=1).astype(np.float32)\n\n        # ---- outputs -------------------------------------------------------\n        # choice is not stored; derive it from instruction x outcome\n        outcome_s = trials['outcome'].values\n        side = np.array([SIDE_CODE[x] for x in trials['trial_instruction'].values])\n        choice = np.where(outcome_s == 'ignore', CHOICE_NO_LICK,\n                          np.where(outcome_s == 'hit', side, 1 - side))\n\n        # per-trial values are repeated across bins so all outputs share one array\n        out = np.empty((n_trials, len(OUTPUT_NAMES), N_BINS), np.int8)\n        out[:, 0, :] = choice[:, None]\n        out[:, 1, :] = np.array([OUTCOME_CODE[x] for x in outcome_s])[:, None]\n        out[:, 2, :] = np.array([EARLY_CODE[x] for x in trials['early_lick'].values])[:, None]\n        out[:, 3, :] = tongue_output(nwb, go)\n\n        # ---- neural --------------------------------------------------------\n        # spike_times is ragged: read the buffer once instead of one read per unit\n        offs = np.asarray(units['spike_times'].data)\n        allst = np.asarray(units['spike_times'].target.data)\n        starts = np.concatenate([[0], offs[:-1]])\n\n        edges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\n        rates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\n        for r, u in enumerate(good):\n            s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n            # running spike total at each edge; (Follow Decoder Task section)\\n  - How to discretize continuous outputs (Follow Decoder Task section)\\n  - Which inputs/outputs should be **time-varying** vs **per-trial** (Follow Decoder Task section)\\n  - How does the reference code load and manipulate this data?\\n  - When possible, import or copy code from the reference code in `/app/code` directory. \\n- Consult CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Steps 1-4 and reference materials to determine:\\n  - Temporal binning for spike rates (if applicable)\\n  - Temporal alignment of trials\\n  - Data filtering and curation rules for neurons, trials, and sessions\\n  - Brain regions recorded from\\n- Mapping should be consistent with CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Steps 1-4.\\n- Check for variables indicating valid data periods — exclude invalid data\\n- Note all decisions, edge cases, and data quality issues\\n- Plan and document **sanity and consistency checks** based on dataset size information from the reference texts, code, and data\\n\\n**Done when**:\\n- You have a complete mapping document in CONVERSION_NOTES.md specifying every source-to-target variable mapping under \\\"Step 5\\\"\\n- You have documented all decisions under \\\"Step 5\\\"\\n- You have documented sanity and consistency checks under \\\"Step 5\\\"\\n\\n**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 6, update Step 5 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 6: Script Development\\n\\n**Goal**: Write the conversion script to `/app/convert_data.py`.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Write all conversion code in the file `/app/convert_data.py`\\n- Script should run as **`python -u /app/convert_data.py <outpicklefile>`**\\n- Include options:\\n  - `--full` (default): Process all sessions\\n  - `--sample`: Process only 2 sessions for testing\\n  - `--show-processing`: Plot visualizations of EVERY processing step for up to 2 sessions. Save plots as `processing_<session_id>.png`.\\n- Reuse code from reference code bases where appropriate\\n- Use `pynwb` to interface with the data. Do not directly load and parse the `hdf5` files with `h5py`.\\n- Write efficient code:\\n  - Vectorize loops\\n  - Avoid unnecessary file I/O\\n  - Use parallel processing if beneficial\\n  - Print timing information to find bottlenecks\\n- Plots for `--show-processing` mode should visually convince the user that every step of the conversion is correct.\\n  - There are no temporal misalignments\\n  - Discretization of continuous outputs is correct\\n- Write clear, well-documented functions\\n- Handle missing data appropriately (consult references, use sensible defaults, document)\\n- Validate data shapes and types at each step\\n- Include sanity checks (e.g., trial counts match across arrays)\\n\\n**Done when**: `/app/convert_data.py` exists and runs efficiently without errors.\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 7 until `/app/convert_data.py` exists and you have updated Step 6 in CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\\n\\n**Goal**: Validate the conversion on a small sample before processing the full dataset.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. Run `python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing 2>&1 | tee /app/conversion_sample_out.txt`\\n  a. Verify the sample data structure matches the specification.\\n  b. Check dimensions are consistent across trials/sessions.\\n  c. Check that no data is missed during conversion. \\n  d. Validate that metadata accurately describes the data.\\n2. Improve efficiency of conversion.\\n  a. Look at and note timing information for the conversion. \\n  b. Estimate how long the full conversion will run. When you do this, make sure that your estimate accounts for differences in lengths/numbers of trials/sessions. \\n  c. If full conversion time estimate is longer than 15 minutes, speed up the code by writing more efficient code (vectorizing loops, removing unnecessary or redundant computations) and/or including parallel processing. \\n3. Run `python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/sample_data.pkl --verify-only 2>&1 | tee /app/verification_sample_out.txt`.\\n4. Analyze the output file `/app/verification_sample_out.txt`:\\n  a. Check input ranges and output value distributions against expectations from reference texts.\\n\\n**Done when**: \\n- `/app/sample_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\\n- `/app/verification_sample_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\\n- Processing plots show no anomalies\\n- Document sample statistics in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 7\\\"\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 8 until `/app/sample_data.pkl` and `/app/verification_sample_out.txt` files exist, and CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 7 is filled in. \\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 8: Sample Decoder Training\\n\\n**Goal**: Verify the decoder runs successfully on sample data.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. Run `python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/converted_data.pkl --full 2>&1 | tee /app/conversion_full_out.txt`\\n4. As the code runs, update your estimates of how long processing will take. If it is much longer than your previous estimate (> 1.5x), kill the process, optimize bottlenecks, and repeat. \\n5. Run `python -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/converted_data.pkl --verify-only 2>&1 | tee /app/verification_full_out.txt`. \\n6. Check that no data was lost during conversion \\n7. Explain why each warning could not be fixed in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 2: Construct sanity checks**\\n- Develop at least one sanity check each on neural, input, and output data.\\n- These must involve loading in the original data files (NOT through your conversion code).\\n- Construct comparison tests and criteria using `np.allclose()`. \\n- These tests can be spot-checks of the data, e.g. neural activity at trial 5, timepoint 10, neuron 3. \\n- Fix all mismatches/sanity check failures. \\n- Document your sanity checks to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 3: Reference code comparison**\\n- Compare your code to the reference code and methods. \\n- For each major processing step — (a) data loading, (b) neuron/trial filtering, (c) temporal alignment, (d) binning, (e) input construction, (f) output construction — identify the corresponding code in your script and in the reference, and compare the logic. \\n- Check whether you use the same variables, filtering, and processing as the reference code. \\n- Fix any mismatches. \\n- Document your comparisons in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n- Explain your reasoning for any differences in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`.\\n\\n**Check 4: Key statistics comparison**\\n- Verify that key statistics (number of animals, sessions, trials, neurons, input and output ranges, output distributions) match information available in the reference papers. \\n- Write code to investigate any discrepancies. \\n- Fix any discovered issues. \\n- Document your comparisons in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 5: Check for edge cases**\\n- Check for off-by-one errors at the beginning/ends of trials, sessions, and subjects, or in definitions of the inputs and outputs. \\n- There may be minor issues in the data that your code must handle. Accuracy results are documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 11\\\" with a table of accuracies\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 12: Critical Review 2\\n\\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Perform all of the following checks:\\n\\n**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\\n- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\\n- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \\n- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \\n\\n**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to papers**\\n- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference papers\\n- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the papers' accuracy for each variable\\n- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \\n- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \\n\\n**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\\n- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \\n\\n**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\\n1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\\n2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\\n3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\\n4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \\n5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and papers. \\n\\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\\n\\n**Report all checks and results** to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 12\\\".\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\\n\\n**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\\n  - Key decisions and rationale\\n  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\\n  - Validation results and tables\\n  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\\n- Create a user-facing `/app/README.md` summarizing:\\n  - Dataset description\\n  - How to load and use the converted data\\n  - Output format specification\\n  - Key statistics\\n- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `/app/cache/` folder\\n- Create `/app/cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\\n\\n**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\\n\\n**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. and video tracking\\n\\nMice performed an auditory delayed response task 21 (Figure 1A). The instruction stimuli during the sample epoch were pure tones played at one of two frequencies (3 kHz or 12 kHz). Each tone was played three times for 150 ms with 100 ms inter-tone intervals. The sample epoch was followed by a 1.2 s delay epoch. An auditory ‘Go’ cue (carrier frequency of 6 kHz with 360 Hz modulating fre-\\nquency, 0.1 s duration) indicated the end of the delay epoch. Licking early during the sample/delay epoch triggered a replay of the epoch. During the response epoch (answer period: 1.5 s) mice reported the instruction by licking one of the two lick ports. Licking (consumption period: 1.5 s) the correct lick port triggered a small water reward (0.1 ~ 0.2 ul). Licking the incorrect lick port triggered a timeout (1-3 s). After mice stopped licking for 1.5 s, the trial ended, followed by a 250 ms inter-trial-interval. Early lick trials and no\\nresponse trials were excluded for analysis. Overall performance was computed as the fraction of correct control trials (i.e. no photostimulation), excluding any early lick trials. We selected experimental sessions for analysis based on following criteria: overall behavioral performance (> 65%), and at least 50 correct lick left and lick right trials each. Mice performed on average 476 (Mean; range, 130-785) trials per session with 84% correct rate (range, 65-99%; STAR Methods). During the delay epoch, mice maintain a memory of their choice and plan a movement.\\n\\nTwo CMOS cameras (CM3-U3-13Y3M, FLIR) were used to track orofacial movements of the mouse under IR light illumination (940 nm LED). The cameras were equipped with 4-12 mm focal length lenses (12VM412ASIR, Tamron) and a pixel resolution of 71 mm. High-speed videos from a side view and a bottom view (Figure 1C) were acquired at 300 Hz using software FlyCapture (TELEDYNE FLIR). We trained DeepLabCut 39 to track the movement of tongue, jaw and nose (Figure 1I).\\n\\nMulti-regional electrophysiological recordings\\n\\nWe designed a ﬂexible manipulator system for multiple Neuropixels probe insertions (https://www.janelia.org/open-science/manipulator-system-for-multiple-neuropixels-probe-recordings). Three to four small craniotomies (diameter, 1 \\u0018 1.5 mm) were made over target brain areas one day before the ﬁrst recording session. Details of recordings made with multiple Neuropixels probes in head-restrained behaving animals have been published (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.8tphwmn). Target regions, insertions angles, probe types, etc. are summarized in Table S2. All coordinates are given with respect to Bregma (AP, anterior-posterior; ML, medial-lateral; DV, dorsal-ventral).\\n\\nExtracellular spikes were recorded using Neuropixels 1.0 probes, 2.0 single-shank (SS) and 2.0 multi-shank (MS) probes 3,4 (Table S2). Three to seven recordings were made from each craniotomy. Recording depth was inferred from manipulator readings (Sensapax uMp manipulators). After completion of probe insertion, brain tissue was allowed to settle for several minutes before recording. During recordings the craniotomies were immersed in saline.\\n\\nProbes were conﬁgured and data were visualized and streamed to disk using the open-source software package SpikeGLX (https://billkarsh.github.io/SpikeGLX/). Data from up to ﬁve simultaneously recorded probes were acquired at 30 kHz. Sync waves (0.5 s duty cycle TTL pulses) were recorded across probes and on auxiliary channels for synchronization.\\n\\nPhotoinhibition\\n\\nLight from two 473 nm lasers (Coherent OBIS LS/LX) was used to illuminate the two hemispheres of ALM. The laser power was controlled by analog outputs controlled by a Bpod (Sanworks). Photoinactivation of ALM (centered on AP 2.5 mm; ML 1.5 mm) was performed through clear-skull cap implant11 or via craniotomy by directing the laser over the skull (beam diameter, 1.8 mm at 4 sigma). Photoinhibition of the left-, right-ALM hemisphere, or both hemispheres was deployed on a subset of ~25% randomly interleaved trials 11,21 (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice). To prevent the mice from distinguishing photostimulation trials from control rials using visual cues, a ‘masking ﬂash’ (1 ms pulses at 10 Hz) was delivered using 470 nm LEDs in front of the mice throughout the entire trial. For silencing ALM, we stimulated cortical GABAergic neurons in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice. We used 40 Hz photostimulation with a sinusoidal temporal proﬁle (5 mW average power per hemisphere) and a 100 ms linear ramping down during the laser offset to reduce rebound neuronal activity. This photo stimulus is expected to silence glutamatergic neurons in all of ALM. 37 We silenced ALM activity during the late delay epoch (last 0.5 s), including the 100 ms ramp-down. Thus, photoinhibition always ended before the ‘Go’ cue.\\n\\nTo analyze the effects of photoinhibition, units with at least 10 photostimulation trials were selected for analysis (Figures 5 and S5). Bilateral ALM photostimulation reduced behavior performance from 83.2% to 71.7% (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, n = 93 sessions). To exclude the effects of rebound population activity in the thalamus 16 and other subcortical regions, we used a 20-120 ms\\ntime window after photo stimulation onset to measure the effect of ALM inactivation in downstream regions (Figures 5 and S5). For ALM itself, we used 500 ms (i.e. the entire inactivation period) to calculate spike rate reduction.\\n\\nSpike sorting and quality control\\n\\nWe developed a data pipeline for preprocessing, spike sorting and quality control (https://github.com/jenniferColonell/ecephys_spike_sorting). The extracellular recording traces were ﬁrst band-pass ﬁltered (Butterworth acausal ﬁlter, 250 Hz - 9 kHz). We then sorted the dataset using both Kilosort2 32 (MATLAB version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/KS20_for_preprocessed_data: Release version of KS2 for preprocessed data) and Kilosort2.5 4 (Python version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/pykilosort: [WIP] Python port of Kilosort 2). Both sorting methods gave similar results. In the analyses presented in the paper, we used the output from Kilosort2. Each output cluster was associated with a list of 15 quality metrics calculated to assess isolation and sorting quality 7 (i.e. quality control) (https://github.com/AllenInstitute/ecephys_spike_sorting/tree/master/ecephys_spike_sorting/modules/quality_metrics).\\n\\nThe details of the spike sorting and quality control are described in an accompanying white paper (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.v1). In brief, we used 15 cluster quality metrics to train classiﬁers - one for each of the major ﬁve brain areas (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain and medulla). The classiﬁers were trained based on labels derived from manual curation. We curated Kilosort2 output (28 penetrations from ﬁve brain areas) using the open-source graphical user interface Phy (GitHub - cortex-lab/phy: phy: interactive visualization and manual spike sorting of large-scale ephys data). Each cluster was labeled as a ‘good’ or ‘unlabeled’ unit. Annotators were blind to location, recording condition and trial type information. Based on the annotated labels of all clusters and associated quality metrics, we trained ﬁve region-speciﬁc classiﬁers using logistic regression. Applying the trained classiﬁers to the rest of the dataset provided lists of units that were labeled as ‘good’ and were used for the analysis in this paper. We applied the cortex classiﬁer to ALM and other cortex, hippocampus, olfactory and cortical subplate units; the striatum classiﬁer to striatum and pallidum units; the thalamus classiﬁer to thalamus and hypothalamus units; the midbrain classiﬁer to midbrain and pons units; the medulla classiﬁer to medulla and cerebellum units. We calculated the rate at which the classiﬁer incorrectly labeled ’unlabeled’ units as ’good’, using 10-fold cross-validation on held-out manually labeled units (false alarm rate): 7.8%; striatum: 6.4%; thalamus: 7.3%; midbrain: 5.5%; medulla 4.3%. This method yielded 8717 good units from ALM, 7664 from striatum, 12808 from thalamus, 7495 from midbrain and 2928 from medulla, etc. Overall, the dataset consisted of 69,943 good units recorded across 173 behavioral sessions, from which 655 probe insertions were made. This corresponds to 25.9 % of clusters reported by Kilosort2.\\n\\n[stdout]\\nBehavior and video tracking\\n\\nMice performed an auditory delayed response task 21 (Figure 1A). The instruction stimuli during the sample epoch were pure tones played at one of two frequencies (3 kHz or 12 kHz). Each tone was played three times for 150 ms with 100 ms inter-tone intervals. The sample epoch was followed by a 1.2 s delay epoch. An auditory ‘Go’ cue (carrier frequency of 6 kHz with 360 Hz modulating fre-\\nquency, 0.1 s duration) indicated the end of the delay epoch. Licking early during the sample/delay epoch triggered a replay of the epoch. During the response epoch (answer period: 1.5 s) mice reported the instruction by licking one of the two lick ports. Licking (consumption period: 1.5 s) the correct lick port triggered a small water reward (0.1 ~ 0.2 ul). Licking the incorrect lick port triggered a timeout (1-3 s). After mice stopped licking for 1.5 s, the trial ended, followed by a 250 ms inter-trial-interval. Early lick trials and no\\nresponse trials were excluded for analysis. Overall performance was computed as the fraction of correct control trials (i.e. no photostimulation), excluding any early lick trials. We selected experimental sessions for analysis based on following criteria: overall behavioral performance (> 65%), and at least 50 correct lick left and lick right trials each. Mice performed on average 476 (Mean; range, 130-785) trials per session with 84% correct rate (range, 65-99%; STAR Methods). During the delay epoch, mice maintain a memory of their choice and plan a movement.\\n\\nTwo CMOS cameras (CM3-U3-13Y3M, FLIR) were used to track orofacial movements of the mouse under IR light illumination (940 nm LED). The cameras were equipped with 4-12 mm focal length lenses (12VM412ASIR, Tamron) and a pixel resolution of 71 mm. High-speed videos from a side view and a bottom view (Figure 1C) were acquired at 300 Hz using software FlyCapture (TELEDYNE FLIR). We trained DeepLabCut 39 to track the movement of tongue, jaw and nose (Figure 1I).\\n\\nMulti-regional electrophysiological recordings\\n\\nWe designed a ﬂexible manipulator system for multiple Neuropixels probe insertions (https://www.janelia.org/open-science/manipulator-system-for-multiple-neuropixels-probe-recordings). Three to four small craniotomies (diameter, 1 \\u0018 1.5 mm) were made over target brain areas one day before the ﬁrst recording session. Details of recordings made with multiple Neuropixels probes in head-restrained behaving animals have been published (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.8tphwmn). Target regions, insertions angles, probe types, etc. are summarized in Table S2. All coordinates are given with respect to Bregma (AP, anterior-posterior; ML, medial-lateral; DV, dorsal-ventral).\\n\\nExtracellular spikes were recorded using Neuropixels 1.0 probes, 2.0 single-shank (SS) and 2.0 multi-shank (MS) probes 3,4 (Table S2). Three to seven recordings were made from each craniotomy. Recording depth was inferred from manipulator readings (Sensapax uMp manipulators). After completion of probe insertion, brain tissue was allowed to settle for several minutes before recording. During recordings the craniotomies were immersed in saline.\\n\\nProbes were conﬁgured and data were visualized and streamed to disk using the open-source software package SpikeGLX (https://billkarsh.github.io/SpikeGLX/). Data from up to ﬁve simultaneously recorded probes were acquired at 30 kHz. Sync waves (0.5 s duty cycle TTL pulses) were recorded across probes and on auxiliary channels for synchronization.\\n\\nPhotoinhibition\\n\\nLight from two 473 nm lasers (Coherent OBIS LS/LX) was used to illuminate the two hemispheres of ALM. The laser power was controlled by analog outputs controlled by a Bpod (Sanworks). Photoinactivation of ALM (centered on AP 2.5 mm; ML 1.5 mm) was performed through clear-skull cap implant11 or via craniotomy by directing the laser over the skull (beam diameter, 1.8 mm at 4 sigma). Photoinhibition of the left-, right-ALM hemisphere, or both hemispheres was deployed on a subset of ~25% randomly interleaved trials 11,21 (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice). To prevent the mice from distinguishing photostimulation trials from control rials using visual cues, a ‘masking ﬂash’ (1 ms pulses at 10 Hz) was delivered using 470 nm LEDs in front of the mice throughout the entire trial. For silencing ALM, we stimulated cortical GABAergic neurons in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice. We used 40 Hz photostimulation with a sinusoidal temporal proﬁle (5 mW average power per hemisphere) and a 100 ms linear ramping down during the laser offset to reduce rebound neuronal activity. This photo stimulus is expected to silence glutamatergic neurons in all of ALM. 37 We silenced ALM activity during the late delay epoch (last 0.5 s), including the 100 ms ramp-down. Thus, photoinhibition always ended before the ‘Go’ cue.\\n\\nTo analyze the effects of photoinhibition, units with at least 10 photostimulation trials were selected for analysis (Figures 5 and S5). Bilateral ALM photostimulation reduced behavior performance from 83.2% to 71.7% (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, n = 93 sessions). To exclude the effects of rebound population activity in the thalamus 16 and other subcortical regions, we used a 20-120 ms\\ntime window after photo stimulation onset to measure the effect of ALM inactivation in downstream regions (Figures 5 and S5). For ALM itself, we used 500 ms (i.e. the entire inactivation period) to calculate spike rate reduction.\\n\\nSpike sorting and quality control\\n\\nWe developed a data pipeline for preprocessing, spike sorting and quality control (https://github.com/jenniferColonell/ecephys_spike_sorting). The extracellular recording traces were ﬁrst band-pass ﬁltered (Butterworth acausal ﬁlter, 250 Hz - 9 kHz). We then sorted the dataset using both Kilosort2 32 (MATLAB version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/KS20_for_preprocessed_data: Release version of KS2 for preprocessed data) and Kilosort2.5 4 (Python version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/pykilosort: [WIP] Python port of Kilosort 2). Both sorting methods gave similar results. In the analyses presented in the paper, we used the output from Kilosort2. Each output cluster was associated with a list of 15 quality metrics calculated to assess isolation and sorting quality 7 (i.e. quality control) (https://github.com/AllenInstitute/ecephys_spike_sorting/tree/master/ecephys_spike_sorting/modules/quality_metrics).\\n\\nThe details of the spike sorting and quality control are described in an accompanying white paper (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.v1). In brief, we used 15 cluster quality metrics to train classiﬁers - one for each of the major ﬁve brain areas (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain and medulla). The classiﬁers were trained based on labels derived from manual curation. We curated Kilosort2 output (28 penetrations from ﬁve brain areas) using the open-source graphical user interface Phy (GitHub - cortex-lab/phy: phy: interactive visualization and manual spike sorting of large-scale ephys data). Each cluster was labeled as a ‘good’ or ‘unlabeled’ unit. Annotators were blind to location, recording condition and trial type information. Based on the annotated labels of all clusters and associated quality metrics, we trained ﬁve region-speciﬁc classiﬁers using logistic regression. Applying the trained classiﬁers to the rest of the dataset provided lists of units that were labeled as ‘good’ and were used for the analysis in this paper. We applied the cortex classiﬁer to ALM and other cortex, hippocampus, olfactory and cortical subplate units; the striatum classiﬁer to striatum and pallidum units; the thalamus classiﬁer to thalamus and hypothalamus units; the midbrain classiﬁer to midbrain and pons units; the medulla classiﬁer to medulla and cerebellum units. This is to deal with cases where for e.g. (bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride is actually 43 but evaluates to 42.999999... due to numerical errors in floating-point arithmetic.\\n    if np.allclose((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride, math.floor((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride)+1):\\n        n_bins =  math.floor((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride)+2\\n    else:\\n        n_bins = math.floor((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride)+1\\n    binCenters = bin_begin_time + np.arange(n_bins)*stride\\n\\n    binIntervals = np.vstack((binCenters-bin_width/2, binCenters+bin_width/2)).T\\n\\n    # Empty 0x1 cell. Need to manually define what it becomes in Python.\\n24\\t2. 1x1 cell. Will be directly read as non-iterables such as str, int, float, etc. Need to manually convert it to an iterable with length 1.\\n25\\t3. Nx1 cell (N >= 2). To view a copy of this licence, visit http://creativecommons.\\norg/licenses/by/4.0/.\\n© The Author(s) 2025\\n\\n===PAGE===\\n\\nNature Neuroscience\\nArticle https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-025-02114-x\\nMethods\\nData collection and preprocessing\\nWe analyzed a publicly available dataset published in refs. 30,31. This \\nstudy is based on data from 28 mice, including 25 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP (The \\nJackson Laboratory, JAX no. 014548), one C57BL/6J ( JAX no. 000664), \\none Sst-IRES-Cre ( JAX no. 013044) crossed with reporter mouse Ai32 \\n( JAX no. 024109) and one Emx1-IRES-Cre ( JAX no. 005628) crossed \\nwith R26-LNL-GtACR1-Fred-Kv2.1 reporter mouse ( JAX no. 033089). \\nThe mice were 3–7 months old at the time of recording. All procedures \\nwere in accordance with protocols approved by the Janelia Research \\nCampus Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.\\nThe data were obtained from Neuropixels probes33 used to record \\nextracellular activity in multiple regions of the mouse brain. T o perform \\nspike-sorting, we used Kilosort56 with a custom quality control pipeline \\noutlined in a whitepaper57 (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.\\nv1). We then binned spikes into firing rates with a bin width of 40 ms \\nand a stride of 3.4 ms.\\nIn addition to neural activity, we recorded high-speed (300 Hz) \\nmultiview video of the face, paws and body of the mouse using comple-\\nmentary metal-oxide semiconductor cameras (CM3-U3-13Y3M, FLIR) \\nunder infrared (940 nm light emitting diode) light, with 4–12-mm focal \\nlength lenses (12VM412ASIR, Tamron), achieving a pixel resolution \\nof 71 µm. For analysis, only the side-view frames were used. We used \\nDeepLabCut24 to obtain the positions of the jaw, paws and tongue. We \\nrefer to these positions as markers. We manually labeled about 2,800 \\nframes, and trained the model using this software, and we used the \\nsame model across all sessions. Although these markers were mostly \\nreliable, we found outliers that harmed the prediction of firing rates \\nor animal behavior. We identified outliers by a five-sigma threshold on \\nvelocity across frames and imputed outliers from nearby frames. When \\nthe tongue was occluded while it was in the mouth, as was typically the \\ncase before the response epoch, we set the tongue position to its mean \\nvalue. We note that other choices of specific data imputation method \\ndid not qualitatively affect the results.\\nFurther details regarding the animals, behavior and data collec-\\ntion, including electrophysiology, video tracking, spike-sorting and \\nhistology, can be found in ref. 30.\\nConvolutional autoencoder\\nThe architecture of the convolutional autoencoder we used was \\nsimilar to BehaveNet described in ref. 22. The encoder was composed \\nof an initial convolutional layer, two residual blocks 58 and two fully \\nconnected layers. The initial convolutional layer has 3 × 3 kernel size \\nand 16 output channels and is followed by ReLU activation and a 2 × 2 \\nmax pooling. Each residual block was composed of four convolutional \\nlayers. Each convolutional layer has kernel size 3 and stride 1. The \\nfirst residual block had 16 channels; and the second residual block \\nincreased the channel number to 32 in the first layer. Each convolu-\\ntional layer is followed by ReLU activation and the second residual \\nblock ends with a max pooling with kernel size 4. The input image was \\nresized into a 120 × 112 matrix. The output of the last convolutional \\nlayer was a vector with a length of 288. This output was then processed \\nby the two fully connected layers (288 × 128 and 128 × 16) with ReLU \\nactivation between them yielding the output of the encoder, the \\nembedding vector, with a length of 16. The decoder was a fully con-\\nnected linear layer.\\nWe trained and primarily used session-specific autoencoders. \\nHowever, we also verified that one can train a session-independent \\nencoder with session-dependent decoders. We note that decoders had \\nto be session-dependent due to differences in overall position of the \\nmouse, experimental components and background. In other words, \\nduring training, all frames are fed into the same encoder but will then go \\nto different decoders depending on which session they were extracted \\nfrom. We verified that training a session-independent autoencoder \\nwith 40 sessions yielded similar performance and qualitatively similar \\nanalysis results to a session-dependent decoder. We also verified that \\nthe encoder can then generalize to sessions that the encoder has never \\nseen before.\\nEnd-to-end learning framework\\nIn the end-to-end learning framework, we trained deep neural networks \\nto directly predict neural firing rates. For each session with each brain \\nregion, we trained a neural network. The network was composed of \\nthree residual blocks 58 and a final linear output layer. Each residual \\nblock was composed of four convolutional layers, and each convolu-\\ntional layer was followed by a two-dimensional batch normalization \\nwith epsilon 1 × 10−5 and momentum 0.1. The first convolutional layer \\nof a residual block had kernel size 1 and stride 1; the latter three had \\n3 × 3 kernel size and stride 1. The output of the first residual block had \\n16 channels, and the output of the other two blocks had 32 channels. \\nEach residual block was followed by a two-dimensional max pooling \\nwith a kernel size of 4 and a stride of 4 for down sampling. After each \\nbatch normalization or max pooling, a ReLU activation was applied. \\nAfter the three residual blocks and the max poolings, the output was a \\nvector of length 160. A linear output layer was connected to the end of \\nthe last residual block with output size equal to the number of neurons \\nto be predicted in the session.\\nPrediction of neural activity using embedding or markers\\nWhen predicting neural activity at time t  from embedding vectors \\nor marker positions, we took a 5-frame window of the video and col -\\nlected the respective features at t  − 6.8 ms, t − 3.4 ms, t, t + 3.4 ms \\nand t + 6.8 ms and concatenated these vectors, obtaining a single \\nfeature vector that was 80-dimensional for the embedding-based \\napproach (16 latent dimensions times the 5 neighboring time points) \\nand 15-dimensional for the marker-based approach (3 markers \\ntimes the 5 time points). We then used L2 regularized linear regres-\\nsion (ridge-regression) to predict neural activity at time t . The \\nregularization parameter was obtained through fivefold nested \\ncross-validation. Neurons with low firing rates (below 2 Hz) were \\nexcluded from analyses; the results were not sensitive to the exact \\nvalue of this threshold.\\nTrial selection and cross-validation\\nThe dataset contains trials with photoinhibition, water administration \\nregardless of the animals’ choice (free water trials), early licks and \\ntrials where the animal ignores the lick-spouts. These were excluded \\nfrom all analyses.\\nFor the analyses comparing the three methods (Fig. 2 and Extended \\nData Figs. 2 and 3), we used a single, random train-test split, with balanc-\\ning of the ratio of lick-left, lick-right and correct versus error trials in \\nthe training and test splits. The test split was 64 trials for all sessions, \\nand the same splits were kept across methods.\\nFor analyses involving only the embedding-based meth -\\nods (Figs. 3 –5 and Extended Data Figs. 4–6), we used fivefold \\ncross-validation, stratified with regards to licking direction and cor -\\nrectness across the folds.\\nFor analyses involving behavioral prediction (Figs. 6  and 7 and \\nExtended Data Figs. 7 and 9), we selected only correct trials and used \\n20-fold stratified cross-validation.\\nThalamic nuclei.  For Fig. 3  and Extended Data Fig. 4 the following \\nsubregion definitions were used, based on the Allen ontology: CN, cen-\\ntral lateral nucleus; central medial nucleus; MD, mediodorsal nucleus \\nof thalamus; PC, paracentral nucleus; PO, posterior complex of the \\nthalamus; VAL, ventral anterior-lateral complex of the thalamus; VM, \\nventral medial nucleus of the thalamus; VP, ventral posterior complex \\nof the thalamus; ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus, parvi-\\ncellular part; ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus; ventral \\nposteromedial nucleus of the thalamus, parvicellular part.\\n\\n===PAGE===\\n\\nNature Neuroscience\\nArticle https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-025-02114-x\\nEpoch-averaged explained variance\\nT o calculate epoch average explained variance we first calculated the \\nexplained variance for each time point and test-fold separately. Then, \\nwe rectified the explained variance scores by setting all negative values \\nto 0. After this, the folds were averaged. Finally, we averaged the time \\npoints within the relevant epoch (sample, delay or response). T o avoid \\nedge effects and compare the same time points (for neural activity) \\nacross all time-shifts, we excluded the first and last 150 ms of each \\nepoch when taking the average. We filtered out neurons with very low \\nexplained variances (below 0.01); the results were not sensitive to the \\nexact value of this threshold.\\nIdentifying neurons with reliable firing patterns and poor \\nvideo prediction\\nT o identify neurons with highly reliable spiking patterns across \\ntrials but poor predictions from behavioral videos (as shown in \\nExtended Data Fig. 1), we selected neurons with low epoch-averaged \\nexplained variance (embedding-based response epoch-explained \\nvariance < 0.1), with high correlation between the single-trial firing \\nrate traces and the trial-averaged firing rate pattern (correlation > 0.4) \\nand with low trial-by-trial variability (average across all time points of \\ninstantaneous trial-to-trial firing rate variance < 100 s−2). We have found \\na total of 196 such neurons in the whole dataset. The exact value of these \\nthresholds does not change the qualitative type or the approximate \\nproportion of these neurons found in the dataset.\\nAnalyzing optimal time-offsets\\nWhen analyzing the optimal time-shift between video and neural activ-\\nity, we shift the video by tau (τ ) in time (multiples of 6.8 ms which \\ncorresponds to two frames). Then we repeat the same analysis that \\nwe did when predicting neural activity using embedding vectors \\nfor a large set of possible time-shifts (−102 ≤ τ  ≤ 102 ms): we take the \\nfeatures corresponding to five neighboring frames at t  + τ − 6.8 ms, \\nt + τ − 3.4 ms, t + τ, t + τ + 3.4 ms, t + τ + 6.8 ms; predict neural activity \\nusing ridge-regression for every time point separately; and calculate \\nthe epoch-averaged explained variance for each possible τ time-shift. \\nThe optimal time-shift is the one that maximizes the explained \\nvariance τ* = max_τ(R2(τ)). Since some neurons’ explained variance \\ncurves as function of time-offset were flat, we kept only neurons with \\nwell-defined peaks (max(R2) ≥ 1.2mean(R2), where mean(R2) is the mean \\nexplained variance across all time-shifts); the results were not sensitive \\nto the exact value of this threshold.\\nT o assess the significance of a neuron’s time-offset (Fig. 5 ), we \\nused the explained variances from the different cross-validation folds \\nand compared the optimal time shifts coming from the different folds \\nagainst zero, using a t-test to obtain a P value for each neuron. Signifi-\\ncance was established through Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery \\nrate control, with rate parameter Q = 0.05.\\nDefining choice- and uninstructed movement-modulated \\nneurons using video-based choice decoder\\nT o define choice- and uninstructed movement-modulated neurons \\n(Fig. 7 and Extended Data Fig. 9), we used all correct trials and split them \\ninto four groups based on licking direction and the delay epoch video \\nprediction (obtained as described above). Sessions with fewer than \\n20 trials in any of the four groups were excluded. We used regularized \\nlogistic regression either to predict choice while conditioning for video \\nprediction or to predict uninstructed movement type (video prediction) \\nwhile conditioning for choice from average firing rates of single neurons \\nduring the delay epoch. The prediction was characterized by ROC AUC on \\nthe test-fold and the two conditions were averaged in each case, yielding \\na single AUC for choice prediction and another AUC for uninstructed \\nmovement prediction for each neuron. The final AUC for each neuron \\nis the average of the test AUC across all test-folds. The regularization \\nparameter was found through nested leave-one-out cross-validation.\\nA neuron was then grouped as choice- versus uninstructed \\nmovement-modulated if the relevant AUC exceeded 0.65; note that \\nsome neurons have AUC higher than this threshold for both variables.\\nDefining choice-modulated neurons after subtraction of \\nmovement-related activity\\nT o define neurons modulated by choice but unaffected by any unin-\\nstructed movements (Extended Data Fig. 10), we first subtracted the \\npredicted per-timepoint neural activity based on the embedding \\nmethod of each neuron. We then used regularized logistic regression \\nto predict choice from single-neuron residual activity using fivefold \\ncross-validation, with nested cross-validation to find the regulariza-\\ntion parameter. Each neuron’s choice decoding AUC is the average \\ntest-fold AUC across all cross-validation folds. T o classify a neuron \\nas choice-modulated we used the same threshold as for the other \\nmethod, AUC > 0.65.\\nCalinski–Harabasz clustering score\\nThe Calinski–Harabasz index, also known as the variance ratio criterion, \\nis the ratio of the sum of between-clusters dispersion of a measured \\nfeature to the inter-cluster dispersion for all clusters. Higher scores \\nindicate stronger clustering. T o obtain a reference null-distribution \\nfor the Calinski–Harabasz score, we randomly assign the labels (mice) \\nto each data point, and then calculate the score, repeating the random \\nprocess 1,000 times. We assess significance by comparison to this \\nnull distribution.\\nWe used this clustering score two times. In Fig. 6d, we take the \\nAUC from the embedding framework as features and mouse identity \\nas cluster labels. In Fig. 6e, AUCs from the jaw and the nose markers \\nwere used as features, and mouse identity was used as cluster labels. \\nWe note that we used only sessions where the trial type was predictable \\nfrom either jaw or nose (AUC equal to or higher than 0.65) and only mice \\nthat had two or more of such predictable sessions.\\nTesting against spatial discontinuity with nearest-neighbor \\nexplained variance difference distribution\\nT o test whether spatially closer neurons have smaller difference in their \\nexplained variance than expected by chance within thalamus (Fig. 3e), \\nwe first identified neurons within each nucleus and calculated the \\ncumulative distribution function for the explained variance difference \\nbetween nearest neighbors. As a control we randomly shuffled the \\nneurons’ explained variance values within each nucleus separately and \\ncalculated the cumulative distribution function for the explained vari-\\nance difference in the shuffled sample. This \\nstudy is based on data from 28 mice, including 25 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP (The \\nJackson Laboratory, JAX no. 014548), one C57BL/6J ( JAX no. 000664), \\none Sst-IRES-Cre ( JAX no. 013044) crossed with reporter mouse Ai32 \\n( JAX no. 024109) and one Emx1-IRES-Cre ( JAX no. 005628) crossed \\nwith R26-LNL-GtACR1-Fred-Kv2.1 reporter mouse ( JAX no. 033089). \\nThe mice were 3–7 months old at the time of recording. All procedures \\nwere in accordance with protocols approved by the Janelia Research \\nCampus Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.\\nThe data were obtained from Neuropixels probes33 used to record \\nextracellular activity in multiple regions of the mouse brain. T o perform \\nspike-sorting, we used Kilosort56 with a custom quality control pipeline \\noutlined in a whitepaper57 (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.\\nv1). We then binned spikes into firing rates with a bin width of 40 ms \\nand a stride of 3.4 ms.\\nIn addition to neural activity, we recorded high-speed (300 Hz) \\nmultiview video of the face, paws and body of the mouse using comple-\\nmentary metal-oxide semiconductor cameras (CM3-U3-13Y3M, FLIR) \\nunder infrared (940 nm light emitting diode) light, with 4–12-mm focal \\nlength lenses (12VM412ASIR, Tamron), achieving a pixel resolution \\nof 71 µm. For analysis, only the side-view frames were used. We used \\nDeepLabCut24 to obtain the positions of the jaw, paws and tongue. We \\nrefer to these positions as markers. We manually labeled about 2,800 \\nframes, and trained the model using this software, and we used the \\nsame model across all sessions. Although these markers were mostly \\nreliable, we found outliers that harmed the prediction of firing rates \\nor animal behavior. We identified outliers by a five-sigma threshold on \\nvelocity across frames and imputed outliers from nearby frames. When \\nthe tongue was occluded while it was in the mouth, as was typically the \\ncase before the response epoch, we set the tongue position to its mean \\nvalue. We note that other choices of specific data imputation method \\ndid not qualitatively affect the results.\\nFurther details regarding the animals, behavior and data collec-\\ntion, including electrophysiology, video tracking, spike-sorting and \\nhistology, can be found in ref. 30.\\nConvolutional autoencoder\\nThe architecture of the convolutional autoencoder we used was \\nsimilar to BehaveNet described in ref. 22. The encoder was composed \\nof an initial convolutional layer, two residual blocks 58 and two fully \\nconnected layers. The initial convolutional layer has 3 × 3 kernel size \\nand 16 output channels and is followed by ReLU activation and a 2 × 2 \\nmax pooling. Each residual block was composed of four convolutional \\nlayers. Each convolutional layer has kernel size 3 and stride 1. The \\nfirst residual block had 16 channels; and the second residual block \\nincreased the channel number to 32 in the first layer. Each convolu-\\ntional layer is followed by ReLU activation and the second residual \\nblock ends with a max pooling with kernel size 4. The input image was \\nresized into a 120 × 112 matrix. The output of the last convolutional \\nlayer was a vector with a length of 288. This output was then processed \\nby the two fully connected layers (288 × 128 and 128 × 16) with ReLU \\nactivation between them yielding the output of the encoder, the \\nembedding vector, with a length of 16. The decoder was a fully con-\\nnected linear layer.\\nWe trained and primarily used session-specific autoencoders. \\nHowever, we also verified that one can train a session-independent \\nencoder with session-dependent decoders. We note that decoders had \\nto be session-dependent due to differences in overall position of the \\nmouse, experimental components and background. In other words, \\nduring training, all frames are fed into the same encoder but will then go \\nto different decoders depending on which session they were extracted \\nfrom. We verified that training a session-independent autoencoder \\nwith 40 sessions yielded similar performance and qualitatively similar \\nanalysis results to a session-dependent decoder. We also verified that \\nthe encoder can then generalize to sessions that the encoder has never \\nseen before.\\nEnd-to-end learning framework\\nIn the end-to-end learning framework, we trained deep neural networks \\nto directly predict neural firing rates. For each session with each brain \\nregion, we trained a neural network. The network was composed of \\nthree residual blocks 58 and a final linear output layer. Each residual \\nblock was composed of four convolutional layers, and each convolu-\\ntional layer was followed by a two-dimensional batch normalization \\nwith epsilon 1 × 10−5 and momentum 0.1. The first convolutional layer \\nof a residual block had kernel size 1 and stride 1; the latter three had \\n3 × 3 kernel size and stride 1. The output of the first residual block had \\n16 channels, and the output of the other two blocks had 32 channels. \\nEach residual block was followed by a two-dimensional max pooling \\nwith a kernel size of 4 and a stride of 4 for down sampling. After each \\nbatch normalization or max pooling, a ReLU activation was applied. \\nAfter the three residual blocks and the max poolings, the output was a \\nvector of length 160. A linear output layer was connected to the end of \\nthe last residual block with output size equal to the number of neurons \\nto be predicted in the session.\\nPrediction of neural activity using embedding or markers\\nWhen predicting neural activity at time t  from embedding vectors \\nor marker positions, we took a 5-frame window of the video and col -\\nlected the respective features at t  − 6.8 ms, t − 3.4 ms, t, t + 3.4 ms \\nand t + 6.8 ms and concatenated these vectors, obtaining a single \\nfeature vector that was 80-dimensional for the embedding-based \\napproach (16 latent dimensions times the 5 neighboring time points) \\nand 15-dimensional for the marker-based approach (3 markers \\ntimes the 5 time points). We then used L2 regularized linear regres-\\nsion (ridge-regression) to predict neural activity at time t . The \\nregularization parameter was obtained through fivefold nested \\ncross-validation. Neurons with low firing rates (below 2 Hz) were \\nexcluded from analyses; the results were not sensitive to the exact \\nvalue of this threshold.\\nTrial selection and cross-validation\\nThe dataset contains trials with photoinhibition, water administration \\nregardless of the animals’ choice (free water trials), early licks and \\ntrials where the animal ignores the lick-spouts. These were excluded \\nfrom all analyses.\\nFor the analyses comparing the three methods (Fig. 2 and Extended \\nData Figs. 2 and 3), we used a single, random train-test split, with balanc-\\ning of the ratio of lick-left, lick-right and correct versus error trials in \\nthe training and test splits. The test split was 64 trials for all sessions, \\nand the same splits were kept across methods.\\nFor analyses involving only the embedding-based meth -\\nods (Figs. 3 –5 and Extended Data Figs. 4–6), we used fivefold \\ncross-validation, stratified with regards to licking direction and cor -\\nrectness across the folds.\\nFor analyses involving behavioral prediction (Figs. 6  and 7 and \\nExtended Data Figs. 7 and 9), we selected only correct trials and used \\n20-fold stratified cross-validation.\\nThalamic nuclei.  For Fig. 3  and Extended Data Fig. 4 the following \\nsubregion definitions were used, based on the Allen ontology: CN, cen-\\ntral lateral nucleus; central medial nucleus; MD, mediodorsal nucleus \\nof thalamus; PC, paracentral nucleus; PO, posterior complex of the \\nthalamus; VAL, ventral anterior-lateral complex of the thalamus; VM, \\nventral medial nucleus of the thalamus; VP, ventral posterior complex \\nof the thalamus; ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus, parvi-\\ncellular part; ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus; ventral \\nposteromedial nucleus of the thalamus, parvicellular part.\\n\\n===PAGE===\\n\\nNature Neuroscience\\nArticle https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-025-02114-x\\nEpoch-averaged explained variance\\nT o calculate epoch average explained variance we first calculated the \\nexplained variance for each time point and test-fold separately. Then, \\nwe rectified the explained variance scores by setting all negative values \\nto 0. After this, the folds were averaged. Finally, we averaged the time \\npoints within the relevant epoch (sample, delay or response). T o avoid \\nedge effects and compare the same time points (for neural activity) \\nacross all time-shifts, we excluded the first and last 150 ms of each \\nepoch when taking the average. We filtered out neurons with very low \\nexplained variances (below 0.01); the results were not sensitive to the \\nexact value of this threshold.\\nIdentifying neurons with reliable firing patterns and poor \\nvideo prediction\\nT o identify neurons with highly reliable spiking patterns across \\ntrials but poor predictions from behavioral videos (as shown in \\nExtended Data Fig. 1), we selected neurons with low epoch-averaged \\nexplained variance (embedding-based response epoch-explained \\nvariance < 0.1), with high correlation between the single-trial firing \\nrate traces and the trial-averaged firing rate pattern (correlation > 0.4) \\nand with low trial-by-trial variability (average across all time points of \\ninstantaneous trial-to-trial firing rate variance < 100 s−2). We have found \\na total of 196 such neurons in the whole dataset. The exact value of these \\nthresholds does not change the qualitative type or the approximate \\nproportion of these neurons found in the dataset.\\nAnalyzing optimal time-offsets\\nWhen analyzing the optimal time-shift between video and neural activ-\\nity, we shift the video by tau (τ ) in time (multiples of 6.8 ms which \\ncorresponds to two frames). Then we repeat the same analysis that \\nwe did when predicting neural activity using embedding vectors \\nfor a large set of possible time-shifts (−102 ≤ τ  ≤ 102 ms): we take the \\nfeatures corresponding to five neighboring frames at t  + τ − 6.8 ms, \\nt + τ − 3.4 ms, t + τ, t + τ + 3.4 ms, t + τ + 6.8 ms; predict neural activity \\nusing ridge-regression for every time point separately; and calculate \\nthe epoch-averaged explained variance for each possible τ time-shift. \\nThe optimal time-shift is the one that maximizes the explained \\nvariance τ* = max_τ(R2(τ)). Signifi-\\ncance was established through Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery \\nrate control, with rate parameter Q = 0.05.\\nDefining choice- and uninstructed movement-modulated \\nneurons using video-based choice decoder\\nT o define choice- and uninstructed movement-modulated neurons \\n(Fig. 7 and Extended Data Fig. 9), we used all correct trials and split them \\ninto four groups based on licking direction and the delay epoch video \\nprediction (obtained as described above). Sessions with fewer than \\n20 trials in any of the four groups were excluded. We used regularized \\nlogistic regression either to predict choice while conditioning for video \\nprediction or to predict uninstructed movement type (video prediction) \\nwhile conditioning for choice from average firing rates of single neurons \\nduring the delay epoch. The regularization \\nparameter was found through nested leave-one-out cross-validation.\\nA neuron was then grouped as choice- versus uninstructed \\nmovement-modulated if the relevant AUC exceeded 0.65; note that \\nsome neurons have AUC higher than this threshold for both variables.\\nDefining choice-modulated neurons after subtraction of \\nmovement-related activity\\nT o define neurons modulated by choice but unaffected by any unin-\\nstructed movements (Extended Data Fig. 10), we first subtracted the \\npredicted per-timepoint neural activity based on the embedding \\nmethod of each neuron. This \\nstudy is based on data from 28 mice, including 25 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP (The \\nJackson Laboratory, JAX no. 014548), one C57BL/6J ( JAX no. 000664), \\none Sst-IRES-Cre ( JAX no. 013044) crossed with reporter mouse Ai32 \\n( JAX no. 024109) and one Emx1-IRES-Cre ( JAX no. 005628) crossed \\nwith R26-LNL-GtACR1-Fred-Kv2.1 reporter mouse ( JAX no. 033089). \\nThe mice were 3–7 months old at the time of recording. All procedures \\nwere in accordance with protocols approved by the Janelia Research \\nCampus Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.\\nThe data were obtained from Neuropixels probes33 used to record \\nextracellular activity in multiple regions of the mouse brain. T o perform \\nspike-sorting, we used Kilosort56 with a custom quality control pipeline \\noutlined in a whitepaper57 (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.\\nv1). We then binned spikes into firing rates with a bin width of 40 ms \\nand a stride of 3.4 ms.\\nIn addition to neural activity, we recorded high-speed (300 Hz) \\nmultiview video of the face, paws and body of the mouse using comple-\\nmentary metal-oxide semiconductor cameras (CM3-U3-13Y3M, FLIR) \\nunder infrared (940 nm light emitting diode) light, with 4–12-mm focal \\nlength lenses (12VM412ASIR, Tamron), achieving a pixel resolution \\nof 71 µm. For analysis, only the side-view frames were used. We used \\nDeepLabCut24 to obtain the positions of the jaw, paws and tongue. We \\nrefer to these positions as markers. We manually labeled about 2,800 \\nframes, and trained the model using this software, and we used the \\nsame model across all sessions. Although these markers were mostly \\nreliable, we found outliers that harmed the prediction of firing rates \\nor animal behavior. We identified outliers by a five-sigma threshold on \\nvelocity across frames and imputed outliers from nearby frames. When \\nthe tongue was occluded while it was in the mouth, as was typically the \\ncase before the response epoch, we set the tongue position to its mean \\nvalue. We note that other choices of specific data imputation method \\ndid not qualitatively affect the results.\\nFurther details regarding the animals, behavior and data collec-\\ntion, including electrophysiology, video tracking, spike-sorting and \\nhistology, can be found in ref. 30.\\nConvolutional autoencoder\\nThe architecture of the convolutional autoencoder we used was \\nsimilar to BehaveNet described in ref. 22. The encoder was composed \\nof an initial convolutional layer, two residual blocks 58 and two fully \\nconnected layers. The initial convolutional layer has 3 × 3 kernel size \\nand 16 output channels and is followed by ReLU activation and a 2 × 2 \\nmax pooling. Each residual block was composed of four convolutional \\nlayers. Each convolutional layer has kernel size 3 and stride 1. The \\nfirst residual block had 16 channels; and the second residual block \\nincreased the channel number to 32 in the first layer. Each convolu-\\ntional layer is followed by ReLU activation and the second residual \\nblock ends with a max pooling with kernel size 4. The input image was \\nresized into a 120 × 112 matrix. The output of the last convolutional \\nlayer was a vector with a length of 288. This output was then processed \\nby the two fully connected layers (288 × 128 and 128 × 16) with ReLU \\nactivation between them yielding the output of the encoder, the \\nembedding vector, with a length of 16. The decoder was a fully con-\\nnected linear layer.\\nWe trained and primarily used session-specific autoencoders. \\nHowever, we also verified that one can train a session-independent \\nencoder with session-dependent decoders. We note that decoders had \\nto be session-dependent due to differences in overall position of the \\nmouse, experimental components and background. In other words, \\nduring training, all frames are fed into the same encoder but will then go \\nto different decoders depending on which session they were extracted \\nfrom. We verified that training a session-independent autoencoder \\nwith 40 sessions yielded similar performance and qualitatively similar \\nanalysis results to a session-dependent decoder. We also verified that \\nthe encoder can then generalize to sessions that the encoder has never \\nseen before.\\nEnd-to-end learning framework\\nIn the end-to-end learning framework, we trained deep neural networks \\nto directly predict neural firing rates. For each session with each brain \\nregion, we trained a neural network. The network was composed of \\nthree residual blocks 58 and a final linear output layer. Each residual \\nblock was composed of four convolutional layers, and each convolu-\\ntional layer was followed by a two-dimensional batch normalization \\nwith epsilon 1 × 10−5 and momentum 0.1. The first convolutional layer \\nof a residual block had kernel size 1 and stride 1; the latter three had \\n3 × 3 kernel size and stride 1. The output of the first residual block had \\n16 channels, and the output of the other two blocks had 32 channels. \\nEach residual block was followed by a two-dimensional max pooling \\nwith a kernel size of 4 and a stride of 4 for down sampling. After each \\nbatch normalization or max pooling, a ReLU activation was applied. \\nAfter the three residual blocks and the max poolings, the output was a \\nvector of length 160. A linear output layer was connected to the end of \\nthe last residual block with output size equal to the number of neurons \\nto be predicted in the session.\\nPrediction of neural activity using embedding or markers\\nWhen predicting neural activity at time t  from embedding vectors \\nor marker positions, we took a 5-frame window of the video and col -\\nlected the respective features at t  − 6.8 ms, t − 3.4 ms, t, t + 3.4 ms \\nand t + 6.8 ms and concatenated these vectors, obtaining a single \\nfeature vector that was 80-dimensional for the embedding-based \\napproach (16 latent dimensions times the 5 neighboring time points) \\nand 15-dimensional for the marker-based approach (3 markers \\ntimes the 5 time points). We then used L2 regularized linear regres-\\nsion (ridge-regression) to predict neural activity at time t . The \\nregularization parameter was obtained through fivefold nested \\ncross-validation. Neurons with low firing rates (below 2 Hz) were \\nexcluded from analyses; the results were not sensitive to the exact \\nvalue of this threshold.\\nTrial selection and cross-validation\\nThe dataset contains trials with photoinhibition, water administration \\nregardless of the animals’ choice (free water trials), early licks and \\ntrials where the animal ignores the lick-spouts.
